title: WHY DID JESUS SPEAK IN PARABLES? THE TERRIFYING ANSWER MOST PEOPLE NEVER NOTICE
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS SPEAK IN PARABLES? THE TERRIFYING ANSWER MOST PEOPLE NEVER NOTICE
They sounded like simple stories about seeds, sheep, coins, weeds, fathers, sons, servants, weddings, vineyards, lamps, fishermen, and ordinary people.
But Jesus was doing something far more serious than telling memorable stories.
And once you understand why Jesus actually spoke in parables, you may never hear His words the same way again.
Because there is something frightening hidden inside the question the disciples once asked Him:
“Why speakest thou unto them in parables?” — Matthew 13:10, KJV
He could have explained everything immediately.
A farmer walked into a field carrying seed.
Some seed fell beside the road.
Then Jesus said something that almost sounds unnecessary:
“Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.” — Matthew 13:9, KJV
Everyone standing there physically had ears.
So Jesus was obviously talking about something deeper.
There is being close enough to Jesus to hear His voice while remaining far enough from Him that His words never penetrate the heart.
That possibility should disturb every religious person.
Because one of the most dangerous places a human being can stand is close enough to Christianity to recognize its vocabulary while remaining untouched by Christ.
And still have soil inside you where the seed refuses to take root.
That is where the parables become uncomfortable.
The Greek word translated “parable” is παραβολή — parabolē.

The idea involves placing something alongside something else for comparison. Jesus would take something familiar—seed, soil, bread, money, sheep, vineyards, weddings—and place alongside it a spiritual reality.
Earthly pictures opened windows into eternal truth.
But those windows did not produce the same response in everyone.
To some people, a parable became a doorway.
To others, it became a mirror.
And some looked into the mirror and walked away.
When the disciples asked Jesus why He spoke in parables, His answer was astonishing:
“Because it is given unto you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given.” — Matthew 13:11, KJV
The Greek word translated “mysteries” is μυστήρια — mystēria.
This does not mean Christianity is a secret society in which clever people discover hidden codes.
In the biblical sense, a mystery is truth belonging to God that must be revealed by God.
The Kingdom cannot simply be conquered intellectually.
And suddenly the parables stop being cute Sunday school stories.
“Therefore speak I to them in parables: because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.” — Matthew 13:13, KJV
Then Jesus reached backward centuries into the prophet Isaiah.
The Hebrew of Isaiah 6:9 contains the haunting words:
The construction intensifies the act of hearing—hear and keep hearing—yet without understanding.
See and keep seeing—yet without perceiving.
That was the tragedy Jesus was exposing.
The problem was not merely that people lacked information.
Their hearts had become resistant to the truth standing directly in front of them.
The One through whom all things were made was standing within hearing distance.
Yet proximity to Jesus did not automatically produce surrender to Jesus.
And that should make us ask a painful question.
How many times has God spoken to us through His Word while we quietly decided which parts we were willing to obey?
We say we want Jesus to speak...
Until He touches our secret sin.
Until He tells us to love the person who wounded us.
Until He challenges the bitterness we have protected for years.
Until He asks for the room in our heart whose door we have kept locked.
Then suddenly the issue is no longer whether God has spoken.
The issue is whether we actually wanted to hear Him.
That is why the parables are dangerous.
They do not merely ask, “Do you understand this story?”
“What kind of heart are you bringing to Jesus?”
Consider the parable of the sower.
The same seed falls on different soils.
Another receives quickly but has no depth.
Another allows the Word to grow, only to have it suffocated by competing desires.
Another receives it and bears fruit.
And before pointing at anyone else, we should ask:
Maybe you once burned for Christ.
Maybe there was a season when opening your Bible felt like opening a letter from home.
And somewhere between surviving life and chasing life, the voice you once treasured became easier to ignore.
You did not necessarily wake up one morning and decide to abandon Jesus.
You simply allowed other things to become louder than Him.
That is exactly why Christ's parables still reach across two thousand years and grab us by the soul.
The thorns do not have to destroy the seed violently.
They only have to choke it slowly.
And maybe that sentence exposed something.
This hit harder than you expected.
Not because typing a comment saves anyone.
But sometimes confession begins when we stop pretending.
Sometimes another exhausted believer needs to discover that he or she is not the only person fighting to keep faith alive.
And sometimes your honesty becomes the sentence God uses to encourage someone else not to walk away.
There is another side to Jesus' parables that is breathtakingly beautiful.
Jesus did not merely expose hardened hearts.
Mark tells us that Jesus spoke publicly in parables and then, when He was alone with His disciples, explained things to them.
That may be one of the most beautiful pictures of discipleship in the Gospels.
The disciples were not rewarded because they were intellectual geniuses.
Read the Gospels carefully and you will discover how often they misunderstood Him.
Staying close enough to Jesus to keep asking.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this needs to hear tonight.
You do not need to understand everything before coming to Christ.
Come carrying the secret you promised yourself nobody would ever know.
Because Christianity is not the story of impressive people climbing high enough to reach God.
The Gospel is the story of God coming down to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And this is where every parable ultimately finds its center.
The Shepherd searching for the lost.
The King inviting people into His Kingdom.
The Bridegroom whose arrival demands readiness.
The One who would eventually stop telling stories long enough to become the center of the greatest story ever told.
Human beings looked at the Son of God and treated Him like a scandal.
At the cross, Jesus carried sin's judgment.
The innocent One suffered for the guilty.
The Shepherd gave His life for the sheep.
And on the third day, the tomb was empty.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately about becoming slightly better people.
It is about dead people receiving life.
And perhaps that explains why one of Jesus' most unforgettable parables still breaks hearts.
The father sees him from a distance.
The father meets him with grace.
Maybe your story contains chapters you wish could be burned.
Maybe there are decisions you cannot undo.
Things you still cannot forgive yourself for.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more than we could imagine.
But the cross also proves something else:
God's grace is greater than the sinner who comes to Christ in repentance and faith.
Jesus did not die so we could decorate our old lives with religious language.
He died and rose so sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you home.
Grace is not permission to remain in the pigpen.
Grace opens the road back to the Father.
So perhaps the deepest question is no longer:
“What is Jesus saying to me through them?”
Because the parables reveal something about the Kingdom...
but they also reveal something about us.
The lost sheep asks whether we know we are lost.
The unforgiving servant asks whether receiving mercy has made us merciful.
The rich fool asks what possesses our hearts.
The Good Samaritan asks whether our love crosses inconvenient boundaries.
The Pharisee and tax collector ask whether we approach God with pride or repentance.
The prodigal son asks whether we will come home.
The sower asks whether the Word is actually taking root.
And the wise and foolish builders leave us with nowhere to hide.
Jesus says the person who hears His words and does them is like someone building on rock.
That may be the dividing line running through this entire article.
And perhaps you have spent years around Christianity without ever truly surrendering yourself to Christ.
But have you surrendered to Him?
But do you want His Lordship?
No article can answer that question for you.
No pastor can repent for you.
No parent can believe for you.
No church membership can substitute for Christ.
No religious performance can erase your guilt.
Trust the One who died and rose again.
And if you already belong to Christ but your heart has grown cold, stop pretending coldness is maturity.
but because in Christ you have encountered a love worth surrendering everything to.
And when you see someone else's comment, do not treat it like content.
There is a human soul behind that screen.
There may come a night when the noise becomes overwhelming and you need to remember the question Jesus keeps asking beneath every parable:
Do you have ears to hear?
There is another practical way you can help this work continue.
But hear this clearly because biblical integrity matters more than conversion numbers:
It does not purchase God's favor.
It does not make God love you more.
It is not a substitute for obedience to Christ, generosity toward those in need, or faithful giving in the life of the church.
And it should not be called a required biblical tithe.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV

Even invite the unbeliever who is willing to listen.
Because this was never supposed to be about building an audience for its own sake.
It must remain about pointing human beings toward Jesus.
That brings us back to the shoreline.
Maybe that soil is a person reading something you shared.
Maybe someone you tag tonight has been quietly considering giving up.
Maybe someone scrolling Facebook at 2:17 in the morning feels too dirty to pray.
Maybe someone believes the worst chapter of their life has already written the ending.
And perhaps God will use something as ordinary as a shared article to remind them of something eternal:
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because a soul may need the Gospel.
Follow because truth deserves more room in your life than endless noise.
do not merely admire the parable.
Because the most tragic person in Jesus' audience was never the one who did not understand immediately.
It was the one who heard the voice of Christ...
And the most beautiful story is still the sinner who finally turns around and discovers that grace has been calling them home.
Your scandal does not have to write your final sentence when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
